1422.title: Where dharma is, there is victory
1422.hook: a woman stands in a king's hall with his son, he says he doesn't remember her, and she names her witnesses
1422.carry: where dharma is, there is victory
1422.howItsDone: The women of the epics are remembered in retellings, songs, plays and household observances; Savitri, for example, is remembered by some married Hindu women in a vow kept at a banyan tree, and Gandhari's line, yato dharmas tato jayah, stands on the emblem of India's Supreme Court.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the body is the first tool of dharma, with Dhanvantari and a definition of health that doesn't stop at the body. Today, a new week on the summit.
screen: `THE BODY IS DHARMA'S FIRST TOOL.` · `A NEW WEEK ON THE SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: A royal hall, crowded. A woman walks in from the forest with a small boy beside her: Shakuntala, and the king's own son. Years before, in a hermitage, King Dushyanta married her and promised to send for her. He never did. Now he looks straight at her and says he doesn't remember her. The court waits for her to cry, or to leave. In the Mahabharata, she does neither. She tells him who saw.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE KING'S HALL.` → `I DO NOT REMEMBER YOU.` → `SHE TELLS HIM WHO SAW.`

segments.voice: You think you're alone with what you did, Shakuntala tells him, but the ancient one who lives in your heart knows it. And she names the other witnesses: the sun and the moon, wind and fire, earth and sky and water, day and night, and dharma itself. In the epic, a voice from the sky finally confirms her, and the king admits he knew all along; he was afraid of what people would say. Here's the big Hindu idea, said plainly. Dharma, the right order that holds the world together, isn't decided by whoever sits on the throne. It's witnessed. Nothing is done in an empty room. The epics keep handing that truth to women, often at the very moment someone expects them to be silent. Sita, told to stay behind in the palace, argues her way into the forest beside Rama, from duty and from love. Savitri walks behind Yama, Death himself, and what wins her husband back isn't her grief but what she says about the good. And Gandhari. During the war, her son Duryodhana comes to her asking for a blessing of victory. She loves him. She won't say it. She says only: where dharma is, there is victory. Yato dharmas tato jayah. Today that line, in Sanskrit, is the motto of India's Supreme Court. A mother wouldn't bend it for her own son, and a modern court took it as its promise: what's right, not who's strong. Readers hear these women differently, some as devoted first, some as choosing their own road. The texts keep their words either way.
screen: `THE ONE IN YOUR HEART KNOWS.` · `DHARMA IS WITNESSED.` · `SITA, SAVITRI, GANDHARI SPEAK.` · `YATO DHARMAS TATO JAYAH.` · then, large: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and let one choice from this week come to mind, small or large. Picture Shakuntala's witnesses around it: the morning light, the night sky, the ground under your feet, and your own heart, which already knows. No judging, just seeing it in the open. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is, and ask for the strength to choose what's right. If you don't, simply let it be seen.

1423.title: Mira's Lord
1423.hook: a song closes by saying whose it is: the women who signed their own names, and the names they signed
1423.carry: in bhakti, the song belongs to god
1423.howItsDone: The songs of women saints such as Mirabai, Andal and Akka Mahadevi are still sung in homes, temples and gatherings, and some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's wedding song at their own weddings.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: where dharma is, there is victory. Gandhari's line, Shakuntala's witnesses, and the women of the epics given words at the hardest hour.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain. That phrase closes song after song sung in Mirabai's name, like a stamp pressed into wax. Singers call it a chhap. Yesterday's women were given their words by the poets of the epics. The next stretch of the year turned to women whose own words survive, in songs and in a few lines of scripture, sometimes with their names pressed right into them.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR.` → `A STAMP PRESSED INTO WAX.` → `WOMEN IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: This is bhakti, the path of loving devotion, in the words of women who lived it. In bhakti, God isn't an idea to be proved. God is someone you love, by a name you choose and keep repeating. So start with the names they gave their God. Mira's songs end on Giridhar. Akka Mahadevi, in Karnataka, closes her vachanas on the lord white as jasmine. Andal, in Tamil, dreams her whole wedding to the Lord, verse by verse. Then the names they gave themselves. Karaikkal Ammaiyar's tradition says Shiva called her Mother. But in her own hymns she signs as a pey, a ghoul of the cremation ground, dancing near him in the night. She didn't hide the bones. She signed with them. Lal Ded, in Kashmir, let people curse her and others bring her flowers, and said neither could touch her. And some women left questions instead of songs, kept in an Upanishad. Gargi asks Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when she's told to stop, she comes back later with two more. Maitreyi, offered property, asks what she'd do with something that can't make her immortal. One honest turn. With songs that traveled mouth to mouth, nobody can always say which lines go back to the woman herself. Either way, the signature keeps working. Whoever sings a Mira bhajan at a home shrine today steps aside at the end: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord. Many devotees put it this way: you borrow a saint's love for God, until one morning it's your own.
screen: `BHAKTI: GOD, LOVED BY NAME.` · `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEIR GOD.` · `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEMSELVES.` · `THE SINGER STEPS ASIDE.` · then, large: `NOT MY LORD, BUT MIRA'S LORD.`

segments.voice: Choose one name for God that you love, or one these women used: Giridhar, Krishna, Shiva, the Lord. Say it silently on each out-breath, the way a bhakti song comes back to the name at its close. When the mind wanders, come back to the name, without scolding yourself. If you don't pray, rest on a word that means love to you, or simply on the breath.

1424.title: Rama's sandals on the throne
1424.hook: a prince sets his brother's sandals on the throne, and pilgrims still carry their saints' sandals: why Hindus bow to the feet
1424.carry: bowing to the feet honors the one who walked first
1424.tomorrow: A hymn that ends on perhaps
1424.howItsDone: Many Hindus touch the feet of parents, grandparents and teachers to ask their blessing; the Varkari pilgrimage carries the padukas of Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram to Pandharpur each year; and regional observances such as Durga Puja in Bengal, Herath in Kashmir and the Sabarimala pilgrimage in Kerala are kept in their own languages and customs.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: in bhakti, the song belongs to God, from the women who signed their own names, Mira, Akka and Andal.
screen: `IN BHAKTI, THE SONG BELONGS TO GOD.` · `NOT MY LORD, BUT MIRA'S LORD.`

segments.voice: A prince walks into the forest to find his older brother and bring him home to be king. Rama refuses. He gave his word to their father, and he'll keep his fourteen years of exile. So Bharata asks for one thing: Rama's sandals. In the Ramayana, Bharata carries them home on his own head, sets them on the throne, and rules in Rama's name, from a village outside the capital, until his brother returns. Today, the last summit sit on the regions, and a pair of sandals.
screen: `A BROTHER WHO WON'T COME HOME.` → `GIVE ME YOUR SANDALS.` → `SANDALS ON THE THRONE.`

segments.voice: That story sits under a practice Hindus still keep: honoring the feet, and what the feet stand for. The sandals aren't Rama. They mark the road he walked, and the throne he gave up to keep his word. In Maharashtra, the Varkaris live this every year in the rains. Crowds of pilgrims walk to Pandharpur, singing, and at the heart of the procession, in palanquins, ride the silver padukas of their saints, Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram. Not statues. Sandals. The saints walked this road; now the road walks with them. Across India, students honor a guru's padukas, and a child touches a grandparent's feet at a birthday or before a trip, and gets a hand on the head in return: a blessing. Many teachers put the meaning simply. The feet carried that person through a whole life, so you honor the road they've walked and what they bring back from it. The regions this year kept the same instinct in their own words. In Kerala, a pilgrim to Sabarimala carries a two-part bundle on the head, offerings on one side and food for the road on the other, and pilgrims call one another Swami. In Bengal, Durga comes home as Uma, a daughter, and is carried back to the river. In Kashmir, walnuts kept through Shiva's great night are shared with family and neighbors. Each place has its own language and its own saints, and none is ranked above another. But the gesture at the heart of today is one of the oldest: bending low before the one who walked first.
screen: `THE SANDALS MARK THE ROAD.` · `THE VARKARIS CARRY THEIR SAINTS' PADUKAS.` · `A HAND ON THE HEAD: A BLESSING.` · `EACH REGION IN ITS OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `BOW TO THE ONE WHO WALKED FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an elder or teacher whose feet you've touched, or might: a grandparent, a guru, someone who walked a hard road before you. Picture bending down, and their hand resting on your head. Stay there for a few breaths, and silently thank them for one thing they carried to you. If you pray, you can end with a pranam to God, hands together at the heart.

1425.title: A hymn that ends on perhaps
1425.hook: the summit sit, looking back over a year that kept asking questions, from a king in a forest to a hymn that wonders who really knows
1425.carry: in hinduism, asking is part of the path
1425.howItsDone: Hindu traditions keep questions inside their texts: the Upanishads hold dialogues between teachers and questioners, the Brahma Sutra opens with inquiry, and the hymn of creation, with its open last line, is chanted as part of the Rig Veda.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bowing to the feet honors the one who walked first, from Rama's sandals to the Varkaris'. Today, the whole year at once.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `BOW TO THE ONE WHO WALKED FIRST.`

segments.voice: Who really knows? The hymn of creation in the Rig Veda asks it near its end, and then, in paraphrase, says this about the one who watches over everything from the highest heaven: perhaps he knows, or perhaps he does not know. That hymn stands in the scripture, question and all. And from the top of year four, it doesn't sit alone. This whole year kept stopping at questions. Today, the year close, told by the questions it asked.
screen: `WHO REALLY KNOWS?` → `PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.` → `A YEAR OF QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: It opened with one. A king who'd lost his kingdom and a merchant thrown out by his family asked a sage: we know these things have left us, so why doesn't knowing help? The whole Devi Mahatmya is the answer. Then the questions got sharper. The schools of thought asked how anyone knows anything at all, and the path let each answer in its own way. The Vedas asked in their own voice: what covered it, where, in whose keeping? Then came the women, several of them remembered for a question. Gargi asked Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when he told her to stop, she came back with two more. Maitreyi asked what she'd do with wealth that can't make her immortal. There's a name for this in the tradition. The Brahma Sutra, a founding text of Vedanta, opens with one short line: athato brahma jijnasa. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman, the longing to know the ultimate. Not a creed to sign first. A question to ask. That's the big teaching under year four. In Hinduism, honest asking isn't a lapse in faith. It's one of the doors in. A tradition could have kept only the answers. This one kept the questions inside its sacred texts, and some are never closed. The hymn of creation ends on perhaps. So that's year four from the top: the goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the women and the regions, and running through all of them, people asking out loud, and a tradition that kept their questions.
screen: `IT OPENED WITH ONE QUESTION.` · `GARGI AND MAITREYI ASKED.` · `ATHATO BRAHMA JIJNASA.` · `ASKING IS A DOOR IN.` · then, large: `IT ENDS ON PERHAPS.`

segments.voice: Let one real question rise, something you don't know the answer to, about your life, or about God, or about anything, and let it sit beside you the way the hymn lets its last line sit. Each time the mind starts building an answer, come back to the breath, and to the question, still open. If you pray, you can hold it before God, or the goddess, as it is.

1426.title: Ganesha writes the Mahabharata
1426.hook: a poet needs a scribe, and the lord of beginnings takes the pen: why Hindus start with Ganesha
1426.carry: ganesha comes first, at every beginning
1426.howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, Ganesha is honored first at the start of a new undertaking, a journey, a wedding, a school year or a ceremony; many write Shri Ganeshaya Namah at the top of a first page, and some images show him as a scribe with a broken tusk.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, year 4 from the top: in Hinduism, asking is part of the path, and a hymn that ends on perhaps. Today is the last day of year four.
screen: `ASKING IS PART OF THE PATH.` · `IT ENDS ON PERHAPS.`

segments.voice: A poet has a story too long to write down himself, so he asks for a scribe. The one who comes is Ganesha. Tradition tells it this way: Vyasa has the Mahabharata in his mind, and Ganesha agrees to write it on one condition. Once the pen starts, it must not stop. Vyasa agrees, and adds a condition of his own: Ganesha must understand every line before he writes it. A good story for the last day of year four, with year five starting tomorrow, with letters.
screen: `A POET WHO NEEDS A SCRIBE.` → `THE PEN MUST NOT STOP.` → `UNDERSTAND EVERY LINE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Why Ganesha? Because in Hindu practice he comes first. Before a wedding, a puja, a journey, a new house or a new school year, families honor Ganesha before anyone else. He's lord of obstacles, the one who clears them, and in some stories the one who sets them in the path of the proud. He's lord of beginnings, and patron of learning and letters. So it fits that the greatest of the epics begins with him bent over a page. And the bargain is worth hearing. Ganesha's condition: no stopping. Vyasa's: nothing written that isn't understood. Tradition adds that whenever Vyasa needed time, he'd recite a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to pause to work it out. Then the broken tusk. In some tellings, Ganesha's pen breaks mid-story, and rather than break his word, he snaps off his own tusk and keeps writing. That's one reason many images show him with one tusk broken, sometimes holding it like a pen. Other stories explain the tusk differently; this one is the scribe's. And it's why many Hindus write Shri Ganeshaya Namah, salutations to Lord Ganesha, at the top of a first page: a letter, an exam, a new account book at Diwali. Not as a charm. As a way of saying this work is offered, from its first line. Next year opens with Sanskrit for readers: the script, a few sacred words, enough to look at a verse and know it. A scribe's kind of year. It's right to begin it with Ganesha.
screen: `GANESHA COMES FIRST.` · `LORD OF OBSTACLES AND BEGINNINGS.` · `THE PEN MUST NOT STOP.` · `THE BROKEN TUSK, STILL WRITING.` · then, large: `SHRI GANESHAYA NAMAH.`

segments.voice: Begin the way many Hindus begin anything. Hands together, and silently, Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, or simply: Ganesha, be with this beginning. Then, with one fingertip, trace a slow line on your palm, as if writing a single letter, one stroke to a breath. If the mind runs ahead to next year, bring it back to this one line. If you don't pray, let the first stroke be your way of saying: this is offered.
Year four. The goddess, Shiva, the schools, the Vedas, the women and the regions, now walked. And the ranges beyond, waiting. Today's word.

1427.title: Devanagari
1427.hook: a line of letters on a wedding card: why learn to read what already works when it's chanted?
1427.carry: among letters, krishna is the letter a
1427.tomorrow: a line runs across the top of the letters. what's it holding up?
1427.howItsDone: Hindu children and adults learn Devanagari at home, at weekend classes and from teachers who chant verses with them; some begin a new subject or school year by writing their first letters before Saraswati or Ganesha.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha comes first, at every beginning, the scribe whose pen must not stop. Year five starts where a scribe would, with the letters.
screen: `GANESHA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: A wedding card on the fridge. A sticker on a laptop. A line of text under a photo in the family group chat. Letters with a flat bar running along the top, each one hanging from it like laundry on a line. Some people read it at a glance. To others it's a row of beautiful shapes. That script is Devanagari, and year five opens with it. So, one question for today: if a sacred line already works when it's chanted, why learn the letters at all?
screen: `A LINE OF LETTERS ON THE FRIDGE.` → `LETTERS HANGING FROM A BAR.` → `WHY LEARN THE LETTERS AT ALL?`

segments.voice: Here's one answer the tradition gives, from the Bhagavad Gita. In chapter ten, Krishna names the places he can be found: among mountains, among rivers, among seasons. And among letters, he says, I am a. Not a temple, not a star. A letter. Some readers notice something about the script itself. In Devanagari, a consonant written alone is never silent: it carries a short a inside it. Ka, not k. Ga, not g. Unless a small mark takes it away, a is there in the letter, the way the Gita says the divine is there in the world. Then the word for a letter: akshara. It also means the imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The Gita uses it both ways. In chapter eight, the akshara is the highest, the imperishable. In chapter ten, aksharas are letters. So learning to read isn't only homework before the real thing. The letters can be a way in. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. Muslim tradition holds that the first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, were a command to read. In Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." And a few lines on: "Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not." Two traditions, each putting something holy right beside learning your letters. And one honest difference. In the Qur'an's words, God is the one who teaches, and the pen is how. In the Gita's words, Krishna is found in the letter itself.
screen: `AMONG LETTERS, I AM A.` · `A SHORT A INSIDE EVERY LETTER.` · `AKSHARA: A LETTER, THE IMPERISHABLE.` · `READ: WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.` · then, large: `THE LETTERS CAN BE A WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Let a soft, open sound ride out on each breath: a, the way it sits inside ka and ga, mouth relaxed, no effort. Breathe in quietly, sound it on the way out, and let it fade into silence before the next breath. Krishna's letter, said for as long as the bell runs.
Devanagari: the script with the bar along the top, used for Sanskrit, and for Hindi and Marathi too. Its letters are aksharas. Year five's first word.

1428.title: Rama's name on the stones
1428.hook: a bridge of stones that float because Rama's name is written on them, and the bar that holds a name together
1428.carry: writing god's name is itself a prayer
1428.tomorrow: why is one vowel written before the letter it's sounded after?
1428.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep likhita japa notebooks, writing Shri Ram or another name of God line after line, and people learning Devanagari often start by copying letters under a ruled top line, finding the bar first to see where each word begins and ends.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: among letters, Krishna is the letter a, and akshara, a letter that's also what doesn't wear away. Today, a look back along the line.
screen: `AMONG LETTERS, I AM A.`

segments.voice: An army stands at the edge of the sea. On the far side is Lanka, and Sita held there. They need a bridge. In a much-loved telling, sung far beyond the old Sanskrit text, the monkeys write one name on every stone, Rama, and the stones float. Valmiki's own Ramayana gives the building to Nala, a monkey engineer; the floating name is the version many grandmothers tell. And yesterday's question has its answer here. The bar across the top of Devanagari holds a word together. Write राम, Rama, and one line holds the whole name.
screen: `A BRIDGE ACROSS THE SEA.` → `RAMA'S NAME ON EVERY STONE.` → `ONE LINE HOLDS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: That bar is the shirorekha, the head line. The letters of one word hang from it together, and where it breaks, a new word starts. Sanskrit often runs words together by sound, so one bar can carry two or three, but a new reader's first move is the same: find the bars. Now the practice the floating stones point to. It's called likhita japa, written repetition. Japa usually means saying a name of God, or a mantra, again and again, often on a string of beads. Likhita japa means writing it. Many Hindu families keep notebooks filled page after page with Shri Ram, or another name of God, a line at a time, and some offer the full notebooks at a temple. The teaching under it is old. Many bhakti teachers say the name of God and God are not two. The name isn't a label; it carries the one it names. That's why, in the story, the stones float, and why a grandmother's notebook is a prayer, not handwriting practice. Now look back along this week, each day on its own bar. Gandhari: where dharma is, there is victory. Mira signing her Lord's name. Bharata carrying sandals home. A hymn that ends on perhaps. Ganesha's pen that wouldn't stop. Krishna in the letter a. Separate words, and one line under all of them: what's sacred, written down and handed on.
screen: `THE SHIROREKHA HOLDS A WORD.` · `LIKHITA JAPA: WRITING THE NAME.` · `THE NAME CARRIES THE ONE IT NAMES.` · `THIS WEEK, WORD BY WORD.` · then, large: `ONE LINE UNDER THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: If you like, take paper, or just a fingertip on your palm. Write a name of God you love, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, or simply Om, once for each slow breath, the way likhita japa is kept, each one on its own line. If you don't pray, write a word that's sacred to you, and let the writing be slow enough to mean it.
Devanagari, still: letters hanging together from one head line, the line that holds a sacred name whole. Year five's word for a while yet.
